scenes.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
scenes.narration: We are now moving from changing a model's weights to giving it external knowledge at the time of a question. This diagram traces retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, through five steps. On the left, the employee asks about the company's remote-work policy. The application searches trusted external documents, not the model's memory. The relevant passage is selected and inserted into the prompt as context. Then the foundation model uses both the question and that passage to produce the answer shown on the far right, with a reference back to the source. Notice the open-book illustration at the bottom: RAG is like opening the right book while answering, instead of trying to memorize every book beforehand. The slide also reminds us that the organization's data stays outside the model's weights. This means updated policies can be retrieved without retraining the base model. But retrieval is not a correctness guarantee. We still need access controls, relevant passages, and a way to confirm the generated statement is actually supported by the cited source.

scenes.title: RAG Benefits and Limits
scenes.narration: This slide intentionally places the advantages and limitations side by side. On the left, RAG can use fresh proprietary data, so an application can answer from documents that were never part of the model's original training. Updating the source system can update the available knowledge without changing the model's weights. Retrieval can use semantic similarity, not just a matching keyword. And when the application includes source references, users can inspect the evidence. Now look at the purple panel on the right. A poor retrieval result or badly designed prompt can make the whole answer wrong even when the model itself is capable. Two runs can still produce different wording; RAG does not remove the nondeterministic nature of generation. The model may also hallucinate or incorrectly combine passages. The middle example shows the retrieval step before generation for that reason. The orange warning at the bottom is the lesson to remember: RAG reduces the opportunity for unsupported answers; it does not eliminate it. Evaluate retrieval quality and answer groundedness separately.

scenes.title: RAG Retriever and Generator
scenes.narration: Here is a concrete example of the retriever and generator working together. Look first at the original question: which country hosted the tournament twice by 1986? A query encoder converts the question into a numerical representation for search. The archive is searched and candidate documents are ranked on the right. Read the first two results. They point to 1986 and 1970 tournament records, both showing Mexico as host. Lower-ranked records describe other countries and dates. The generator on the far right should not guess from its general memory. Instead, it takes the relevant retrieved evidence and answers Mexico, with the 1970 and 1986 records as supporting sources. Notice the scores beside the candidates. These help with ranking in this search system, but they are not universal probabilities that an answer is correct. A different embedding or index configuration could change the scores. Finally, read the warning across the bottom: if the retrieved documents do not support an answer, the application should communicate that limitation instead of inventing one. This separation between finding evidence and generating prose is central to RAG.

scenes.title: Choose the Right RAG Data Store
scenes.narration: Not every search problem calls for the same kind of storage. This slide gives three distinct requirements. On the left are relationships and recommendations, such as identifying accessories frequently purchased with a particular camera. When traversing connections between products, customers, and purchases matters, a graph-oriented store may be suitable. In the middle, the shopper wants four-K televisions under a price limit, from a specific brand, and in a certain size. Those are exact words and structured filters, so a text or structured search store fits naturally. On the right, the shopper describes a lightweight laptop for college with long battery life. That is an intent expressed in ordinary language; a vector-search store can retrieve products with semantically similar descriptions. Notice the product catalog under the three panels: the same business data can support different kinds of access. The note on the right highlights that Amazon OpenSearch can support lexical search and vector search in one system. When designing a RAG application, decide whether the problem is relationship traversal, exact filtering, semantic retrieval, or a combination before picking a store.

scenes.title: Embeddings: Meaning as Vectors
scenes.narration: An embedding converts text into a numerical vector that a search system can compare. Follow the three examples on the left. Cloud network and VPC routing have related meanings, even though the words are not identical. Garden plants refers to something very different. All three texts pass through the embedding model in the centre, producing vectors in a high-dimensional space. On the right is a simplified two-dimensional picture of that space. The cloud networking examples appear close together, while garden plants is farther away. Real production embeddings can have hundreds or thousands of dimensions; the two axes are just an illustration. This is why semantic search can find relevant text even when the user's wording does not exactly match a document. Remember that an embedding is not a readable answer. It is a representation used for retrieval, clustering, or related comparisons. It is also important to keep the query and document embedding process compatible; otherwise their positions and similarity scores will not be meaningful for the intended index.

scenes.title: Vector Search: Retrieve Nearest Chunks
scenes.narration: Now we connect embeddings to an actual retrieval system. Start with the document chunks on the left. Each chunk is converted to an embedding vector and stored with metadata such as its source, page, section, or other attributes. At step two, the user's question is encoded into a query vector using a compatible embedding model. That vector is sent to the index at step three. The index searches for nearby document embeddings according to a similarity measure. Finally, the right side shows the top three matching chunks, their ranking scores, and the source documents. Notice the highest result is about vector search and returns a score of zero point nine two in this example. The next results have lower scores, but what matters is their relevance to the query, not treating the numbers as absolute confidence percentages. We then pass appropriate passages, not the raw numeric vectors, into the prompt for the foundation model. Practical systems also use metadata filters, access restrictions, reranking, and relevance thresholds so that an apparently similar document does not become an inappropriate answer source.

scenes.title: RAG Example with a Vector Database
scenes.narration: Let's trace this employee-handbook example from left to right. The employee asks where to find parental-leave eligibility rules. Instead of searching a huge handbook manually, the application converts the question into an embedding. The vector store then returns the most relevant handbook chunks. Look at the retrieved passages. The eligibility rules appear at the top, followed by related sections about the application process and leave overview. The application assembles a prompt containing the user's question and this evidence, then sends it to a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock. The answer shown on the right identifies the eligibility section and cites the handbook source. Notice the three handbook pages along the bottom: those source documents are the ground truth for this use case. The model should not present an uncited employment policy from memory when the official handbook is available. This is also where security matters: the application should only retrieve the handbook sections the employee has permission to access. By the end of this workflow, we have transformed an ordinary document collection into a more useful, source-grounded question-answering experience.

scenes.title: RAG in Bedrock: Knowledge Bases
scenes.narration: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases brings together much of the RAG workflow shown on the previous slides. There are two major sections here, marked one and two. First, ingest and build the knowledge base. The sources may include documents in Amazon S3 and supported connected data sources. Documents are split into chunks, transformed into vector embeddings, and stored in a suitable vector store. In this illustration, the chosen store is Amazon OpenSearch Serverless; other supported options shown include Amazon Aurora and S3 Vectors, subject to their capabilities and the chosen configuration. The second half begins when a user asks a question. Knowledge Bases retrieves relevant content, then an Amazon Bedrock foundation model produces an answer using both the user's request and the retrieved context. Look at the dashed arrow running from the vector store to the query workflow: that is the bridge from indexing time to runtime. Notice the configuration callouts for model access and vector dimensions, too. These choices affect compatibility, search quality, cost, and security. For exam scenarios, separate ingestion from retrieval and generation, and identify which component owns each responsibility.

scenes.title: Using Knowledge Bases
scenes.narration: This slide shows how a knowledge base supports a real employee question. The user asks about the company's remote-work policy. Above the main flow is the knowledge base itself, containing HR policies, an employee handbook, IT guidelines, and benefits information. These documents are indexed for retrieval through the vector-search service shown on the right. At query time, the retrieval component finds relevant excerpts based on the question. Those excerpts flow to Amazon Bedrock, which produces the grounded answer displayed on the far right. Notice that the answer includes citations to specific policy and handbook pages. This allows the employee to check the original documents rather than taking the model's statement on faith. Now read the two boxes below the flow. An application can integrate the knowledge base through Bedrock's APIs, while agents can use knowledge bases as part of a larger task-oriented workflow. Those are different integration patterns, but the same principle applies: provide the model with trusted evidence when it needs company-specific facts. Before launching this system, verify access boundaries, document freshness, retrieval relevance, and how citations are presented to the user.

scenes.title: Create a Knowledge Base
scenes.narration: Here is a practical six-step setup walkthrough. Begin at the top left by choosing your source documents in Amazon S3. Next, select an embedding model to represent the document chunks numerically. At step three, choose the vector store that will hold those embeddings; this example shows Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. Step four is particularly important: configure chunking, which decides how large the retrieved pieces will be and how much context they carry. Step five synchronizes and indexes the source documents so the knowledge base can search them. Only after that do we reach step six: ask a test question and inspect the retrieved results. Follow the lower arrow back toward the left, where the example shows a security best-practice question and the returned passages. The checklist underneath calls out IAM permissions, encryption, and testing both retrieval and output quality. A knowledge base that was created successfully in the console is not necessarily a knowledge base that retrieves the correct evidence. For a real application, test actual user questions, review access permissions, and resynchronize data when the underlying documents change.

scenes.title: The Retrieval Stages in RAG
scenes.narration: We finish this section by breaking RAG into five separate retrieval and generation stages. Number one is pre-retrieval, where content may be extracted, cleaned, chunked, indexed, and the query may be prepared or rewritten. This affects what the search system can find in the first place. Number two is retrieval: the vector or search index returns candidate passages for the user query. Number three is post-retrieval, where the application can filter and rerank those candidates, removing low-value or irrelevant chunks. The fourth stage augments the prompt by combining the original user request with selected supporting context and instructions. Finally, at number five, the foundation model generates the answer using that augmented prompt. Look across the bottom of the slide. Every stage has its own explanation of why quality depends on it. If the source data is poorly chunked, the right passage may never be indexed. If retrieval is weak, reranking cannot always rescue it. If the prompt is assembled badly, the model may ignore useful evidence. The goal is not just to build a pipeline that runs, but one where each stage can be measured and improved. Next, we'll go deeper into chunking and retrieval quality.
